newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - Woolworth sees Eastbay buy accretive.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Woolworth sees Eastbay buy accretive.

text.p: Woolworth Corp said on Monday that it agreed to acquire catalog retailer Eastbay Inc for $24 a share and it expects the deal to be accretive to its financial results in the first year.

"We expect (the acquisition) will be accretive in our fiscal 1997, which will be the first year of the transaction," Roger Farah, chief executive officer of Woolworth, said in a telephone conference call.
Mike Conn, an analyst with Gruntal & Co, agreed.
"Given the track record of Eastbay...it seems very likely that the acquisition will be additive," he said.
Conn believes the acquisition could add as much as four to five cents a share to Woolworth's earnings, but the cost of the acquisition will moderate earnings accretion in 1997.
"We have to assume some goodwill cost, as well as closing costs in the first quarter," Conn cautioned.
Farah said that Woolworth anticipates accelerating growth at Eastbay, which would complement Woolworth's athletic business, beyond its historic levels.
"We have expectations that the performance of this business will move along quicker in the next five years than the last five years," Farah said.
According to Woolworth, from June 1992 to June 1996, Eastbay sales grew at a compound annual rate of 30.6 percent.
Eastbay, which sells athletic shoes, apparel and equipment through catalogs to target customers 12 to 24 years old, had operating income for the fiscal year ended in June of $8.3 million.
Earlier this year, Greenway Partners unsuccessfully sought to separate Woolworth's profitable Foot Locker division and Champs athletic stores from the rest of Woolworth's retail operations.
Many analysts had felt the spin-off proposal, which was defeated at the company's annual meeting in June, would have damaged the remainder of the company.

"I see this as a good acquisition for Woolworth. It gives them a new distribution channel and the ability to tap into a wider assortment of athletic apparel and equipment...that would not be stocked in a Champs or Foot Locker," said David Toung, retail analyst with Argus Research.
"The atheltic business has always been good to Woolworth," he said. Farah said Eastbay and Woolworth's athletic group will each have access to the other's inventory.
Currently, about 25 percent of the product of the two businesses overlap.
"We think that one of the advantages that we bring to Eastbay is access to product," Farah said.

"If you think about the dynamics of their ability to use, through the right technology, our overall inventory investment of over $1.5 billion, we in fact, can help the fulfillment rate of their catalogs, hopefully right out of the box."
Farah expects inventory turnover at Eastbay to increase from twice a year now. Inventory of the athletic group turns over three to four times a year.
According to Farah, there is also an opportunity to improve vendor terms at Eastbay.
Toung also felt Woolworth would help Eastbay develop its mailing lists.
"Woolworth stores will get a customer list (for Eastbay). This is a very good way to develop Eastbay's mailing list," he said.
Eastbay shares rose 4-1/4 to 23-1/4, while Woolworth was unchanged at 24 in afternoon trade on Monday.
